candidates.title: Transferability of Generate–Validate–Repair Pipelines to Large Multi‑Vendor Topologies
candidates.research_question: How well does a generate–validate–repair pipeline for LLM-driven network-configuration changes transfer from emulated benchmarks to larger, multi-vendor simulated topologies without increasing outage or regression risk relative to a human-curated baseline?
hypotheses: When applied to larger multi-vendor topologies, generate–validate–repair pipelines will exhibit a higher regression rate than reported on small emulated benchmarks.
Augmenting generate–validate–repair with topology-aware constraints and vendor-aware templates will reduce regression rate by ≥30% compared to an unconstrained generate–validate–repair pipeline.
candidates.proposed_design: Preregistered comparative study using public topology templates and vendor configuration families: (1) build three topology scales (small/emulated baseline, medium heterogenous, large heterogenous) using network simulators/emulators (ns-3/mininet + vendor-template artifacts). (2) Implement three interventions: human-curated baseline, unconstrained generate–validate–repair pipeline (LLM→syntactic validator→repair loop), and constrained generate–validate–repair with topology- and vendor-aware constraints. Validators include reachability and access-control checks (deterministic). For each of 120 intent-to-change tasks per topology scale, record produced configs, validator outputs, repairs, and replay connectivity tests. Fix seeds and model prompts; limit retries per preregistration.
candidates.expected_data: Per task and pipeline: produced configuration artifacts, binary validator pass/fail, number of repair iterations, post-deployment replay connectivity results (connectivity matrix), regression indicators (new outages or ACL regressions), outage durations (simulated), and validator-flagged safety violations.
candidates.primary_outcome: Difference in regression rate (proportion of tasks causing any connectivity or policy regression) between constrained generate–validate–repair and unconstrained generate–validate–repair on large heterogeneous topologies.
candidates.analysis_outline: Compute regression rates with 95% bootstrap CIs per pipeline and topology scale. Use paired comparisons (McNemar or paired proportion test) across identical task instances to test hypothesis of ≥30% reduction. Report effect sizes and exact p-values. Perform subgroup failure-mode analysis by vendor and topology feature; report repair iteration distributions and validator false negatives/positives.
risks: Generate–validate–repair performance may degrade at larger scale and introduce new regressions (EF2).
Simulator/emulator fidelity may not capture production device quirks leading to optimistic safety estimates (UQ1, CG1).
Agentic components may be vulnerable to prompt-injection or hallucination propagation if used in orchestration (EF3).

candidates.title: Defensive Patterns against Tool‑Selection and LLM‑as‑Judge Prompt‑Injection in Weakly‑Constrained NetOps Agents
candidates.research_question: Which defensive architecture patterns (constrained tool surface, independent tool-verifier, authenticated tool‑handoff) most reliably reduce successful tool-selection and LLM-as-judge prompt-injection attacks in weakly-constrained agentic NetOps workflows?
hypotheses: A constrained tool-surface combined with an independent tool-verifier will reduce successful tool-selection attacks by ≥50% compared to an unconstrained agent.

Adding an authenticated tool-handoff protocol (signed tool outputs validated by a separate verifier) will further reduce attack success while keeping operational false-positive rates acceptable (<10%).
candidates.proposed_design: Adversarial evaluation framework: construct a minimal agentic NetOps orchestration with LLM planner, tool registry (configuration appliers, validators, monitoring), and optional defenses. Implement adversary strategies from the literature (prompt-injection, tool-selection manipulation, malicious tool descriptions). Compare four arms across identical attack corpora: baseline (no defenses), constrained tool-surface, independent tool-verifier, and constrained+verifier+authenticated-handoff. Use 500 randomized attack attempts and 500 benign tasks; measure attack success, benign task success, latency overhead, and false positives. Fix prompt families and random seeds per preregistration.
candidates.expected_data: Per attempt: attack/benign label, agent tool selection trace, tool inputs/outputs, verifier decisions, whether the attacker achieved unauthorized tool invocation or incorrect judgment, task success, and latency metrics.
candidates.primary_outcome: Reduction in attacker success rate (proportion of attack attempts resulting in unauthorized tool invocation or malicious action) for the constrained+verifier+handoff arm vs baseline.
candidates.analysis_outline: Compute attacker success rates with 95% CIs per defense arm; compare arms with exact binomial tests and compute risk ratios. Report defender false-positive rates on benign tasks and latency trade-offs. Conduct attacker-adaptive follow-up experiments on top-performing defenses to assess robustness.
risks: Adaptive adversaries may craft inputs that bypass the verifier or mimic legitimate tool descriptors (EF3, UQ2).
Defenses may introduce unacceptable operational latency or false positives, degrading operator trust and availability.
Defense evaluation on simulated tools may not fully represent production tool complexity (external validity concern).

candidates.title: Confining LLMs to Translation and Delegating Constraint Solving to Formal Solvers for Safer NetOps Changes
candidates.research_question: Does an architecture that confines the LLM to intent-to-spec translation and delegates constraint solving to a formal solver (SMT/constraint optimizer) reduce operational regressions relative to end-to-end LLM planning for configuration generation?
hypotheses: A translator+solver pipeline will produce fewer operational regressions than an end-to-end LLM planner on the same set of intent-to-change tasks.
Translator+solver will have higher determinism (lower output variance) across repeated prompts than end-to-end LLM planning, improving verifier trustability.
candidates.proposed_design: Controlled A/B pipeline experiment: implement (A) end-to-end LLM planner that outputs concrete configuration sequences and (B) LLM translator that emits formalized constraints/specification fed to a solver (e.g., Z3 or standard constraint optimizer) which synthesizes configurations. Use 200 intent-to-change scenarios across multiple topology templates and policy constraints. Validators (reachability, ACL semantics) run post-synthesis. Record solver unsat cases and compare regression rates, success rates, and per-task variance across 5 prompt seeds.
candidates.expected_data: Per scenario and pipeline: synthesized configuration, validator pass/fail, regression indicator, solver unsat count, number of prompt trials per scenario, and variance of outputs across seeds.
candidates.primary_outcome: Difference in regression rate (validator-detected regressions) between translator+solver and end-to-end LLM planner across scenarios.
candidates.analysis_outline: Estimate regression-rate differences with bootstrap CIs; use paired proportion tests for significance. Quantify output variance across seeds (entropy or edit distance) and compare distributions (Kolmogorov–Smirnov). Analyze unsat cases to characterize specification gaps and propose mitigations.
risks: Formal solvers may produce no-solution (unsat) cases, requiring human fallback or conservative defaults (CG3).
Solver models require accurate domain models; drift between solver model and real device semantics can produce incorrect but solver-legal outputs (construct validity).
Integration latency and engineering complexity may limit real-time applicability.

candidates.title: Prompt‑Governance and Prompt‑Averaged Estimands for Reliable NetOps Measurement
candidates.research_question: How do prompt-family governance and prompt-averaging affect measured performance, uncertainty quantification, and construct validity of LLM-driven intent-to-configuration translation tasks in NetOps evaluations?
hypotheses: Prompt-averaged estimands produce wider but better-calibrated confidence intervals for operational correctness than single-prompt evaluation.
Applying prompt-governance to limit admissible prompt families will reduce measured performance variance without materially degrading median operational correctness.
candidates.proposed_design: Methodological experiment defining three prompt families (conservative, neutral, exploratory) constructed via controlled template transformations. For a fixed set of 200 tasks, sample 50 prompts per family and collect LLM outputs. Compute single-prompt estimates, prompt-family medians, and full prompt-averaged estimands (weighted by governance weights). Evaluate operational correctness via deterministic validators and replay tests. Assess CI calibration (coverage) and estimator variance; preregister prompt-family construction, sampling scheme, and governance weights.
candidates.expected_data: Per task and prompt: prompt identifier, raw model output, validator pass/fail, replay connectivity outcome, and metadata. Aggregated per-task prompt-averaged success rates, per-family medians, CI widths, and coverage statistics.
candidates.primary_outcome: Calibration and width of 95% confidence intervals for operational correctness under prompt-averaged estimands vs single-prompt estimates (measured by empirical coverage across tasks).
candidates.analysis_outline: Compute empirical coverage of 95% CIs via bootstrap across tasks for each estimator. Compare CI widths and variances using paired tests; report changes in median correctness and variance under governance-weighted averaging. Perform sensitivity analysis over governance weights and prompt-family definitions.
risks: Prompt-family choices and governance weights are subjective and may affect conclusions (construct validity, CG4).
Sampling enough prompts increases model-call cost and may still underrepresent adversarial prompt variants (UQ3).
Findings on synthetic/emulated tasks may not fully transfer to production scenarios (external validity).

candidates.title: Efficacy of Phase‑Gated Troubleshooting Policies for LLM‑Agent NetOps Workflows
candidates.research_question: Do phase‑gated, structured agent policies (diagnose→isolate→repair→verify) materially improve correctness and safety of LLM-agent troubleshooting workflows compared to unstructured prompting on operational NetOps troubleshooting tasks?
hypotheses: Phase-gated policies will increase successful fault resolution rate by ≥25% compared to unstructured LLM prompting on the same troubleshooting tasks.
Phase-gated policies will reduce dangerous repair actions (those producing regressions) by ≥30% relative to unstructured prompting.
candidates.proposed_design: Controlled comparison using a public NetOps troubleshooting task set (NIKA-like problems): implement two agent workflows — (A) unstructured LLM prompting and (B) phase-gated policy enforcing explicit stage outputs and stage-specific validators. For 300 troubleshooting cases, run both agents with identical observation inputs. Record resolution success, number/type of repair actions, validator-flagged safety violations, and number of tool invocations. Fix prompts and policy templates in preregistration.
candidates.expected_data: Per case and agent: stage transcripts, proposed repairs, applied configurations, validator outcomes, whether original fault resolved, any introduced regressions, and counts of tool calls.
candidates.primary_outcome: Difference in successful fault-resolution rate between phase-gated policy agent and unstructured prompting agent.
candidates.analysis_outline: Compute resolution rates and regression rates with 95% CIs. Use paired proportion tests for significance. Report stage-level error rates, median number of repair iterations, and qualitative failure-mode taxonomy. Include ablation of individual phase constraints to identify high-impact components.
risks: Structured policies may overconstrain the agent, reducing flexibility on novel faults (construct validity).
Agent transcripts and tool interactions could be susceptible to prompt-injection or tool-manipulation attacks if not guarded (EF3).
Benchmarked troubleshooting tasks may not cover rare real-world failure modes (external validity).
